_comment: THE shared behavioural contract for the field-lifecycle and blackout RPCs.
Round 2 made the mock and the migration one contract for the affected-booking
KIND LITERALS, by parsing them out of the migration text. That worked because
the literals are text in one file. RPC BEHAVIOUR is not: it lives in PL/pgSQL
on one side and JavaScript on the other, and no amount of parsing turns one
into the other. So round 2's fixes to admin_retire_field and
admin_unretire_field landed in the SQL and not in the mock, and round 3 found
both -- one of them CERTIFIED by a passing test.
A per-field diff would not have caught them either; the next divergence is a
field nobody thought to diff. What is shared instead is the OUTCOME: this file
lists cases and what each must produce, and both implementations are run
against it and asserted to agree with THIS, not with each other.
* tests/fieldLifecycleScenarios.test.js   runs them against the mock client
* scripts/dbharness/scenarios.py          emits SQL that runs them against
Postgres, invoked by run.sh
Dates are relative to the day of the run, as offsets in days from today, so
both sides compute the same absolute date and no scenario expires. `null` is
an unbounded window. Every field named here is pseudonymous.
Breaking either side must fail the case, in both harnesses. That is proved:
scripts/dbharness/prove.sh plants against the SQL and the mutation sweep
against the mock.
REFUSAL CONTRACT. A scenario expecting `ok:false` names the SQLSTATE it must
be refused WITH, in `expect.sqlstate`. Both runners check it, so a row
refused for an unrelated reason -- the caller lost its admin role (42501), or
the field id did not resolve (P0002) -- fails instead of scoring as a pass.
The JS runner used to accept ANY error while the SQL runner restricted the
class, so five blackout cases could have stopped exercising their constraint
and stayed green. The mock now carries `error.code`, which is what PostgREST
puts there, so one contract is expressible for both.
DELETE SCENARIOS (LIVE-1). `admin_delete_field` had no booking guard at all;
it now carries the one `admin_retire_field` already had. Its cases add two
keys the retirement cases do not need: `bookings`, the kinds to seed on the
field before the call, and `expect.deleted`/`expect.exists`, because a
deletion's outcome is whether the row survives rather than what its columns
say. `expect.auditPhases` is stated on every accepted field case -- a refused
delete records `refused` where an accepted one records `before` and `after`,
and hard-coding that in each runner is how the two came to disagree before.
What these cases do NOT cover, stated rather than left implied: what happens
to each booking ROW after a confirmed delete -- the two CASCADE kinds
destroyed and the two SET NULL kinds kept and unassigned. That is schema
behaviour rather than RPC outcome, and it is pinned in
docs/sql/20260907000000_smoke.sql, supabase/tests/field_delete_booking_guard.sql
and tests/fieldDeleteGuard.test.js. A refusal writing NOTHING is covered here,
on both runners, because that is the guard's whole promise.
WHAT A DELETE COSTS IS THE CASCADE CLOSURE, NOT A COLUMN NAME. The first
version of these delete cases enumerated the seven tables carrying a
`field_id` and reported one disposition per TABLE. Both were wrong, and a
review caught them: `games` carries no field_id and is destroyed anyway
(it hangs off game_slots ON DELETE CASCADE), and an assignment reaches the
field a second way through its slot columns -- CASCADE where field_id is
SET NULL -- so the row the SCHEDULER writes is destroyed while a
free-standing one survives. The `scheduled_game` and `scheduled_practice`
booking kinds seed the shape persist_game_schedule and
persist_practice_schedule actually produce, and `delete-mixed-shapes-refused`
puts both shapes on one field so a per-table answer cannot pass.
A NULL CONFIRMATION IS NOT A CONFIRMATION. `retire-null-confirm-refused` and
`delete-null-confirm-refused` pass `p_confirm => NULL` on both RPCs. `NOT NULL`
is NULL in SQL, so a bare `NOT p_confirm` leaves the refusal unfired and the
destructive path runs unconfirmed -- which admin_retire_field did until
20260907000000, while the mock refused it. The one input that turns the guard
off is now covered on both arms rather than on whichever happened to be right.

fieldScenarios.why: A retirement dated ahead leaves the field live until it arrives.
A retirement already in the past deactivates on the spot.
Inclusive on the end date: retired FOR today is still live today.
HIGH 1. Retiring something is not a way to un-deactivate it. The mock wrote active:true unconditionally and handed a deactivated field back to the scheduler.
Same, with a past date: still false, by both terms of the conjunction.
Re-retiring an already future-retired field moves the date and keeps it live.
Clears the date; the field was live and stays live.

HIGH 2. The field is inactive BECAUSE the retirement passed. Unretire clears the date and leaves activity alone -- it cannot know whether the deactivation was the retirement's doing. Re-activating is admin_update_field.
HIGH 2, the sharpest form. Nobody ever retired this field; it was simply switched off. Unretiring it must not switch it back on. The suite asserted active===true here and so certified the bug.
The no-op direction. An active, undated field is unchanged.

`expect.ok` was shape-validated on all 19 scenarios and read by neither runner for a field scenario -- a field parsed and never read, in the table whose premise is that both runners read it identically. It is load-bearing now: this is the one field case that must be REFUSED, so an `ok` branch that vanished would fail here.

LIVE-1. Ground nothing is booked on deletes with no confirmation. Without this case the guard could be 'refuse everything', which satisfies every refusal case below and is not the contract -- admin_delete_field keeps existing because a genuine mistake still needs a delete.

LIVE-1. game_slots.field_id is ON DELETE CASCADE, so the slot is destroyed with the field. One kind per case: an arm dropped from the RPC's five-way union fails the case for THAT table rather than being absorbed by the others.

LIVE-1. game_assignments.field_id is ON DELETE SET NULL, so a FREE-STANDING assignment -- one with no slot behind it -- survives having silently lost its venue. Its slot-linked twin is the next case, and the two must report DIFFERENT dispositions.
LIVE-1. practice_slots.field_id is ON DELETE CASCADE.

LIVE-1, the sharpest form. practice_assignments.field_id had NO foreign key at all, so a delete left the uuid DANGLING at a row that no longer exists -- worse than SET NULL, because nothing downstream could tell it from a live venue. This is the free-standing shape; the slot-linked one follows.

One FREE-STANDING booking in each of the four tables that carry a field_id, and p_confirm true. The count must be 4: the game slot here has no fixture on it, so the games arm contributes nothing and a union that lost an arm reports 3. Both disposition words must appear, because the two slot tables cascade and the two unlinked assignments are merely unassigned.

The shape persist_game_schedule actually writes: a game slot, an assignment carrying game_slot_id, and a games row. All three are DESTROYED, because the slot cascade reaches the assignment before field_id's SET NULL can fire. Reporting 'unassigned' here -- which the first version of the RPC did for the whole table -- promises the operator a survival that does not happen.
The same for practices: a practice slot and an assignment carrying practice_slot_id and slot_id, both ON DELETE CASCADE to practice_slots. Both destroyed, neither unassigned.

Both shapes on one field, so BOTH disposition words must appear in one refusal. A version that reported per TABLE rather than per ROW can satisfy either single-shape case above by picking the right constant; it cannot satisfy this one.

`p_confirm => NULL` must read as UNCONFIRMED. `NOT NULL` is NULL, so a bare `NOT p_confirm` leaves the IF unfired and the retirement proceeds with nobody having confirmed -- which is what the SQL did until 20260907000000 while the mock refused it. A three-valued flag guarding a destructive action must read unknown as no. The field must be untouched and the only audit phase must be `refused`.
The same input on the delete arm, so the guard's weakest input is covered on both RPCs rather than on whichever one happened to get it right.

The org gate, on the delete arm as well as the retire arm. A SECURITY DEFINER RPC bypasses RLS, so this check is the only thing between an admin of one organisation and another's ground -- and a guard that refuses bookings while letting a stranger through would be worse than none.

THE BOUNDARY, STATED AS DATA. `p_after` is the last day the ground is usable -- the reading `field_is_live_on(effective_to, d) = effective_to >= d` already ships -- so a game slot dated EXACTLY on the retirement date is not stranded and the retirement proceeds. This case exists because the SQL and the mock shared an off-by-one on `practice_assignments` (comparing a daterange's EXCLUSIVE upper bound), and two agreeing implementations compared only to each other cannot see that. One pair per arm, because a single arm getting it right by accident is exactly the state this table was in.

The other side of the same boundary, and the positive control for the case above: a game slot dated ONE DAY after the retirement date IS stranded, so the retirement refuses and the field is untouched. Without it, an enumerator that had stopped seeing this kind entirely would pass the on-boundary case for the wrong reason.

blackoutScenarios.why: Minutes past midnight, both bounds present.
num_nonnulls(location_id, field_id) = 1: exactly one, never both.
The reason is a closed enum, so free text cannot arrive through it.
Both minutes or neither; one alone is a window with no other end.
